content: Salvia hispanica, commonly known as chia, is a plant belonging to the genus Salvia within the mint family. It is native to the central valley of Mexico. Chia is cultivated commercially for its seeds, which are highly rich in omega-3 fatty acids. The term chia originates from the Aztec word chian, which translates to oily. The Mexican state of Chiapas derives its name from the Nahuatl phrase meaning chia water or chia river. The species was given the name hispanica (meaning of Spain) because it was first described by Carl Linnaeus based on cultivated plants in Spain. Chia is an annual herbaceous plant that can grow up to one meter in height. Its leaves are arranged oppositely and measure 4–8 cm in length and 3–5 cm in width. The plant produces purple or white flowers, which grow in dense clusters on spikes at the ends of its stems. Chia seeds are small, oval-shaped, and approximately one millimeter in diameter. They exhibit a mottled coloration, including shades of brown, gray, black, and white. Nutritionally, chia seeds contain about 20% protein, 34% oil, and 25% dietary fiber, most of which is soluble and of high molecular weight. They are also rich in antioxidants, including chlorogenic acid, caffeic acid, myricetin, quercetin, and kaempferol flavonols. Chia seeds are naturally gluten-free and contain only trace amounts of sodium. Importantly, no toxic components have been identified in chia seeds. Traditionally, chia seeds have been consumed in Mexico, the southwestern United States, and South America, although they are not widely recognized in Europe. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) considers chia a food with a well-established history of safe consumption. Historically, chia seeds were a staple food for the Nahuatl (Aztec) cultures of central Mexico. Jesuit chroniclers noted that chia was the third most important crop for the Aztecs, following corn and beans, and ahead of amaranth. Chia seeds were often used as a form of tribute and taxation paid to the Aztec priesthood and nobility. Today, chia is commercially cultivated in its native Mexico as well as in Bolivia, Argentina, Ecuador, and Guatemala. A related species, golden chia, is used similarly but is not widely grown for commercial purposes. Chia seeds can be consumed raw as a source of dietary fiber and omega-3 fatty acids. When ground, the seeds produce a meal known as pinole, which can be used to make porridge or cakes. Chia seeds soaked in water or fruit juice are also commonly consumed, particularly in Mexico, where the preparation is known as chia fresca. The soaked seeds develop a gelatinous texture and are used in gruels, porridges, and puddings. Ground chia seeds are incorporated into baked goods such as breads, cakes, and biscuits. Additionally, chia sprouts are used in salads, sandwiches, and other dishes in a manner similar to alfalfa sprouts.
